summary: Generate, score, and spec candidate 2-player games to reach 10 total in the SnapLover games hub
logs: Selected 8 games for full spec: Connect Duo, Edge Letters, Fleet Siege, Duo Quiz, Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, Copy Cat, Reflex Match, Bingo

selected.name: Connect Duo
selected.mechanic: A shared 7x6 grid where players alternate dropping a disc into a column; gravity resolves it to the lowest open row. Fully deterministic with no hidden information and no randomness at all, so the entire game state is just an append-only synced log of column-index messages (one message type, idempotency-guarded against double-processing) — both sides render identically and run the same 4-in-a-row win-check locally off that log, so no message ever needs to carry a verdict, only a move.
selected.rationale: Lowest build effort of the whole slate combined with top-tier engine fit: zero randomness, zero secret state to protect, a single trivial message type, and true alternating turns are actually the correct mechanic here rather than a shortcut — it satisfies every hard constraint (no shared RNG needed, no turn-gating debate) almost by construction. Ships first as a fast, near-zero-risk way to prove out the widened 'hub' concept before tackling anything with more state or a fairness design.

selected.name: Edge Letters
selected.mechanic: Each round, both players privately pick one letter at the same moment — one player a start letter, the other an end letter — and reveal them to each other via one paired network exchange with no ordering dependency, so neither side is ever waiting on the other. Once both letters are known on both devices, players race to type any real word that begins with the start letter and ends with the end letter; the first valid submission wins the round, best-of-5 wins the match. Validity is checked independently and identically on both devices against the bundled word list and the two-letter constraint (the same normalize/validate helper pattern already shared across the app's word games), so a submission never needs to be trusted over the network — each client only trusts its own local check, and the winner's claim is simply verified by the other side against the same rule.
selected.rationale: This is the user's own mandatory pick, and it turns out to match one of the AI-generated pool concepts (Bookends) almost exactly — merged here rather than kept as a separate entry, using Bookends' fully fleshed-out simultaneous-reveal-then-race design to spec it. It reuses the existing word-list/validation infrastructure almost as-is, tying for the best engine fit in the slate at very low effort, so it slots in right after the cheapest board game.

selected.name: Fleet Siege
selected.mechanic: Reuses Word Sonar's 'secret info never leaves the device' architecture, spatial instead of lexical: each player privately places a fixed fleet (sizes centralized in shared game config) on their own grid, and the layout itself is never transmitted, only referenced locally. Players alternate firing a coordinate at the opponent's board — true alternating turn-gating is correct here, since each shot's value genuinely depends on reading the opponent's prior results — and the receiving side computes hit/miss/sunk from its own board state and replies with only that result, exactly like Word Sonar's letter-owner computing the answer locally rather than exposing the source data.
selected.rationale: Directly reuses Word Sonar's already-proven 'owner computes the answer locally' pattern with almost no new architecture, giving it top engine fit at low effort, plus zero rules-learning cost since nearly everyone already knows Battleship. Tied on build effort with Edge Letters but its grid UI is slightly newer surface than a two-letter word race, so it lands just behind.

selected.name: Duo Quiz
selected.mechanic: A static trivia question bank (JSON, identical in both app bundles, no server needed) ships with the app. One peer is the sole round authority: it locally shuffles question order and broadcasts only the current question's text/choices via a single message, so both peers see the same prompt at the same instant with no turn-gating on answering — both respond immediately and independently. Correctness needs no network trust at all, since the right answer is baked into the same static bundle both devices already hold: each peer grades its own submission locally and simply relays true/false for a shared scoreboard, and the authority peer advances rounds via an idempotency-guarded 'next round' message — the same double-click guard lesson already learned twice from earlier games' next-round desync bugs.
selected.rationale: High engine fit at low effort — the part that sounds like it needs fairness engineering (fair content selection) collapses to 'ship the same static bundle to both clients and let each grade itself,' with the one genuinely reusable safeguard (idempotent round-advance) already a proven pattern rather than new design work. Fourth because its surface area (question bank content, scoreboard UI) is marginally larger than the two-letter and grid games ahead of it.

selected.name: Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe
selected.mechanic: A 3x3 grid of 3x3 tic-tac-toe boards. Players alternate placing symbols; whichever cell a player plays within their local board dictates which of the 9 sub-boards the opponent must play in next (if that board is already won or full, they may play in any open board). Winning a sub-board claims it as a mark on the outer meta-board; three sub-boards in a row on the meta-board wins the game. Fully deterministic with zero randomness needed — true alternating turn-gating is correct here, since each move's legality strictly depends on the prior move — so one message per move (board index, cell index) with an idempotency guard against double-processing is enough, with win-check logic run identically and independently on both sides from the synced move log.
selected.rationale: The user's own mandatory pick. Architecturally simple in the same append-only-log sense as Connect Duo (no shared RNG, no secret state), but the meta-board/active-board legality rules add noticeably more UI and state-machine work — tracking 9 sub-board states, the 'active board' highlight, and forced-any-board fallback — than the flatter games ranked above it, which is why it lands mid-pack despite matching them on engine fit.

selected.name: Copy Cat
selected.mechanic: Rounds alternate a Poser/Mimic role by round-index parity (deduced identically on both sides, never transmitted — the same trick as Doodle Duel's drawer alternation). The Poser strikes any pose or expression on camera and hits capture, reusing the existing capture-frame.ts and chunked image-transfer.ts pipeline to send the still to the Mimic. The Mimic gets a short prep window with the reference photo shown as a semi-transparent ghost overlay on top of their own live camera feed, then hits capture for their own attempt; both stills are shown side by side, and — exactly like Doodle Duel's single-authority judging — only the Poser rates the result, since only they know what they were actually going for.
selected.rationale: The one concept that plays directly to SnapLover's unique existing strength (camera plus synced capture) rather than being a generic 2-player game bolted on, and it reuses two already-hardened pipelines (frame capture, chunked image transfer) instead of building new ones. Placed sixth because its real build cost is new UI — ghost-overlay compositing, side-by-side reveal, rating flow — not new network or fairness design, which keeps it a notch behind the purely logic-driven games above it.

selected.name: Reflex Match
selected.mechanic: A round-alternating authority (deduced by parity, never transmitted) picks a small integer seed and sends it once at round start. Both clients deterministically render an identical grid of simple procedural shapes from that seed — reusing the app's existing 'paint from pure config, no image assets' approach already used for photo-strip frames — with one cell always the odd one out by a shared deterministic derivation from the same seed, so both sides compute it identically without it ever being singled out over the network. Using the already-solved clock offset from the app's clock-sync module (the same primitive driving the photo countdown), both clients reveal the grid at one synced timestamp; each side timestamps its own tap locally and sends it immediately, and the round's authority peer is the sole arbiter comparing both synced timestamps to declare the winner.
selected.rationale: A genuinely elegant reuse of the clock-sync primitive already battle-tested for the photo countdown, repurposed for a competitive reflex duel — architecturally sound, with one seed message and one authority-side comparison covering all the fairness needs. Ranked seventh rather than earlier because the synced-reveal-instant requirement plus procedural shape rendering are new enough surface area to cost more than the pure logic-log games, even though the design itself is low-risk.

selected.name: Bingo
selected.mechanic: Directly resolves the shared-randomness problem flagged as the hard part of this concept, the same way Doodle Duel resolved word-picking: single authority per round. Each player privately generates their own 5x5 card locally at round start (a personal card, never transmitted, so there's nothing to keep in sync at that step). One peer, chosen by round parity, is the sole caller for that round: they hold a locally shuffled 1-75 draw order and broadcast one number at a time on a short interval, and both sides mark their own card against that same broadcast stream, so there is nothing left to desync. First to complete a line sends a claim, which both sides — not just the caller — can verify independently against the numbers actually broadcast so far; caller role flips next round.
selected.rationale: The user's own mandatory pick, and per the original brief the one flagged as 'genuinely tricky' given the no-shared-randomness constraint — it needs a full single-authority-per-round design (never sharing a card, only an append-only broadcast draw stream) plus a claim-verification path both sides can check independently, rather than a simple move-log. That extra fairness design work, not any lack of engine fit, is why it is sequenced last despite being a required deliverable.

specs.name: Connect Duo
specs.rules: Standard Connect Four, played on a 7-column × 6-row grid (42 cells), rendered identically on both screens. Players alternate turns; on your turn you pick one of the 7 columns and your disc drops to the lowest currently-empty row in that column (gravity — never a free placement). First player to align 4 of their own discs in a row — horizontal, vertical, or either diagonal — wins immediately. If all 42 cells fill with no such alignment, it's a draw. A column that is already full (6 discs) cannot be picked; this is enforced purely client-side (the column's drop-affordance is disabled the instant its height reaches 6, computed identically on both sides from the shared move log) so an illegal move is never even sendable, let alone something the network protocol has to reject. The host (room creator / WebRTC initiator) always plays the first disc; the guest always plays second — fixed once, at room creation, by the existing generic isInitiator flag already used for host-authority elsewhere in the codebase, not by a dedicated message. There is no setup phase, no secret information, and no randomness anywhere in the rules: every fact about the game (board state, whose turn it is, whether/how someone has won) is 100% public and 100% derivable by both peers from the same ordered list of past moves.
specs.turnModel: Strict alternating exclusive turns, and — unlike Word Sonar's full-word guess — this is the correct mechanic here, not a UX shortcut being taken for convenience. Word Sonar's guess-vs-ask split exists because a full-word guess is an action the guesser can attempt at any moment without needing information from the opponent's next move; gating it on "whose turn" would only add artificial waiting. Connect Duo has exactly one action type (drop a disc in a column) and the entire game IS the alternation: letting a player drop two discs before the opponent's reply would materially change the game's outcome, not just its pacing, because the board is the single shared piece of state both players are reasoning about turn-by-turn. So turns are gated at two layers: (1) UI — the column drop-targets are disabled entirely for the side whose turn it is not, computed from moves.length % 2 vs. local isInitiator; (2) network — on receiving a connectduo-move, each side checks that its `index` equals the receiver's own moves.length (the expected next ply) before appending it, and silently drops anything that doesn't match (stale replay, out-of-order delivery, or a future bug reintroducing a double-send) rather than trusting the sender's turn-taking blindly.
specs.singleAuthority: No single authority is needed over any piece of game state during play — that's the whole appeal of this mechanic. There is no randomness to generate and no hidden information one side must compute on behalf of the other (contrast Word Sonar, where whoever is asked must be trusted to score their own secret word honestly). The two places "authority" language even applies are both trivial and resolved without a dedicated message: (a) who moves first — fixed permanently at room creation by the existing isInitiator flag (host = first mover = e.g. coral discs), the same convention already used for drawerIsInitiatorForRound in Doodle Duel; (b) whose "Rejouer" click wins a near-simultaneous double-click race — it doesn't matter, because connectduo-rematch is idempotency-guarded (monotonic id + a local ref-guard), so whichever message either side's local processing observes first is the one both sides converge on, and the loser of the race is simply ignored as a duplicate. Win/draw detection is never adjudicated by either peer "on behalf of" the other: it's a pure function of the shared move log, run independently and identically on both machines, so there is structurally nothing to arbitrate.
messageTypes: { t: "connectduo-hello" } — sent once by the guest as soon as its message listener is attached, mirroring photo's hello/config handshake and Doodle Duel's duel-hello. The host must not send its first connectduo-move until this arrives, closing the exact 'listener not attached yet on a freshly-mounted React instance' race this codebase has hit and fixed twice already.

{ t: "connectduo-move"; index: number; column: number } — the ONLY move message, and the entire durable game state. `index` is the 0-based ply number: index % 2 === 0 is always the host's disc, odd is always the guest's (identical parity trick to drawerIsInitiatorForRound, but per-move rather than per-round, and used both to color the disc and to validate turn order on receipt). `column` is 0–6. Appended to a local append-only array exactly twice total per move — once optimistically by the sender at click-time, once by the receiver on delivery — and never re-sent, corrected, or acknowledged with a reply. Board contents, next mover, and win/draw state are all pure functions of this array alone, so no verdict ever needs to travel on the wire.

{ t: "connectduo-rematch"; id: number } — sent by whichever side clicks 'Rejouer' first after game-over. `id` is a monotonically incrementing rematch counter, same guard pattern as duel-next-round's `round` and mindmatch-advance's index, paired with a local rematchAdvancedRef so a near-simultaneous click from both sides (or a stray double-fire) resets the board exactly once instead of racing two independent resets.
syncPitfalls: Turn-gating is the correct mechanic here, not a repeat of the Word-Sonar guess-gating mistake: the game's only action (drop a disc) is genuinely exclusive-alternating because both players are editing the same public board, unlike a full-word guess that doesn't need to wait on the opponent's next move to be valid.

Rematch uses the duel-next-round / mindmatch-advance idempotency-guard pattern (monotonic id + ref-guard) precisely because 'Rejouer' is a button both sides can click independently at any moment — the same desync class already found twice in this codebase (Doodle Duel's un-networked 'next round' click, then rediscovered and fixed proactively in Mind Match) would otherwise reappear a third time here.

No message ever carries a win/draw verdict, by design: both sides run the exact same win-check function over the exact same append-only move log after every append, so consistency is structural rather than trusted — this avoids a whole bug class where a stale or buggy peer could assert a winner the other side's independently-computed board disagrees with.

Column-full checks and 'whose turn is it' must both be recomputed from the shared move log itself (moves.filter/length), never cached in a second mutable 'heights' array or a separate turn-counter state variable that could quietly drift out of sync with the log — one source of truth, always derived, never a second structure that can rot.

Received messages are still turn-validated (index === receiver's own moves.length) even though the sender-side UI already disables out-of-turn moves — cheap defensive symmetry against a stale reconnect replaying an old message or a future regression, on top of (not instead of) the UI-level gate.

The message-listener effect mounts once on `[dataChannel]` (same shape as use-capture-session's config ref and use-duel-session's word/round refs) — anything it reads (current move log, expected next index) must come from a ref kept fresh by a companion effect, or moves after the first would validate against permanently-stale state from mount.

No game-state resume on reconnect, matching Doodle Duel and Word Sonar's existing scope: signaling has zero notion of 'game', so a peer that drops mid-game and rejoins starts with an empty local log — a disconnect surfaces the same generic 'partner disconnected' room state as the other games, not a Connect-Duo-specific replay; called out explicitly here so it isn't silently assumed away during implementation.
specs.uiNotes: Board renders on the existing dark game-screen treatment (matches the sombre lobby/séance pattern, not the light landing/result pattern) — a `#161319`-toned frame with 42 circular cutouts, empty holes showing the paper/cream background color, filled holes showing a disc. Two disc colors reuse only existing theme tokens and deliberately avoid violet (reserved exclusively for marking the "join" path per the Doodle Duel convention — "jamais utilisé ailleurs"): host discs in coral (#fb5a46), guest discs in ink (#1c1712), both flat fills, no gradients (gradients on this surface are reserved for the coral duel/hub promo blocks). Each column has an invisible full-height drop-target button above the board; hovering (desktop) previews a ghost disc at the top of that column in the mover's color, but only when it is the local player's turn and the column isn't full — otherwise the whole column is inert (no hover feedback), making "not your turn" and "column full" visually indistinguishable-by-design from "you can't act here right now," which is the correct read for both. Placing a disc animates it falling from the top of the column to its resolved row with a short Framer Motion spring (~250–300ms, ease-out-with-slight-bounce to sell "gravity" without becoming a gadget animation) — only the newly-placed disc animates; existing discs never re-render/re-animate. Turn indicator sits above the board as a small text line with a disc-colored swatch ("À toi de jouer" / "Au tour de Partenaire"), reusing the generic "Toi"/"Partenaire" labeling and the existing `FaceBubbles.tsx` component for the persistent camera bubbles (same as Doodle Duel/Mind Match — no name capture, no config screen, just a "Créer une partie" button). On win, the 4 winning discs get a subtle pulse/outline (no confetti-tier effect, consistent with the codebase's "sobre" animation rule) and a result banner appears ("Tu as gagné !" / "Partenaire a gagné" / "Égalité") with a "Rejouer" CTA. A downloadable/shareable recap (final board + result, composed on canvas like `compose-recap.ts` in the other two games, reusing `lib/share-or-download.ts`) would fit the established Wordle-adjacent shareability pattern well, but is a natural v1.1 addition rather than required for the first ship — flagging it rather than building it silently, since the priority here is proving the hub concept fast with the lowest-risk mechanic.

specs.name: Edge Letters
specs.rules:
SETUP: kind "edge-letters", prefix "E" (free — existing prefixes are P/photo, D/duel, W/word-sonar), routes /edge-letters, /edge-letters/join, /edge-letters/r/[code], root component EdgeLettersClient.tsx, registry entry added to lib/games/registry.ts exactly like the duel/word-sonar entries (icon: SpellCheck2 from lucide-react, promoNamespace "landing.edgeLetters"). No prénom, no config screen — generic "Toi"/"Partenaire" labels, same scope choice as Doodle Duel/Word Sonar/Mind Match: host clicks "Créer un duel" and that's it.

MATCH: config.edgeLetters.rounds = 5, always played to completion even if the match is mathematically decided early (same simplicity-over-early-stop convention as Doodle Duel/Word Sonar — no early termination logic to get wrong). Each round: (1) picking — both players privately pick ONE letter each, one assigned the "start" role and one the "end" role for that round; (2) racing — once both letters are known on both devices, both players see "STARTS WITH ⟨X⟩ · ENDS WITH ⟨Y⟩" and race to submit any real word matching both constraints, completely untorn-gated; (3) reveal — the round's winner (or a no-winner draw on timeout) is shown; (4) advance to next round or, after round 5, recap. Final score header (wins-wins, draws don't count for either side) decides the match; a tie is possible and shown as "Match nul" in the recap.

ROLE ASSIGNMENT (start vs end letter each round): pure function of round parity, deduced identically on both devices, never transmitted — startPickerIsInitiator(round) = round % 2 === 0, exact same pattern as Doodle Duel's drawerIsInitiatorForRound and Word Sonar's askerIsInitiatorForRound. Over 5 rounds each player gets the start-letter role and the end-letter role roughly evenly (3/2 split, alternating).

LETTER PICKING: UI shows a 26-tile A-Z grid, header labelled with the player's role this round ("Choisis la lettre de DÉBUT" / "Choisis la lettre de FIN"). Tapping a tile locks it in immediately and sends it — no "confirm" step, no ordering dependency: each side sends its own pick the instant it's chosen, and independently flips itself to the "racing" phase the moment BOTH its own pick and the peer's pick are known (exact same dual-readiness-flag pattern as Word Sonar's myWordReady/peerWordReady → maybeStartPlaying, cited in the app's own prior art as the way to avoid one side waiting on message order). config.edgeLetters.pickDurationMs (generous, ~15s, same "don't create false time pressure" lesson learned from Doodle Duel/Word Sonar) is a purely LOCAL soft timer — if a player hasn't picked when it expires, their own client auto-picks a random unpicked... any random A-Z letter for them and sends it through the normal message; no network coordination needed for this fallback since only the side that's late needs to act.

RACING: free-text input, Enter or a submit button. Local validation gates everything BEFORE any network traffic: normalizeWord(word) must (a) exist in the bundled French word list, (b) start with the round's start letter and end with the round's end letter (compared via normalizeWord so accents/case never block a legitimate match), (c) be at least 2 characters (blocks the degenerate 1-letter-word case when start letter happens to equal end letter). Invalid attempts never touch the wire at all — pure local rejection with inline UI feedback, a deliberate simplification versus Word Sonar (whose guesses always have to go over the network because only the peer holds the secret word to check against; Edge Letters needs no opponent secret, so bad guesses cost nothing). Once a submission passes local validation, the client locks itself out (no further submissions this round) and sends its claim. config.edgeLetters.raceDurationMs (generous, ~45s) starts the instant both clients enter "racing"; if it elapses with no valid claim from either side, the round resolves as a draw (see sync pitfall on symmetric timeout below).

WORD LIST: new shared infrastructure this game requires (doesn't exist yet in the codebase) — a bundled, statically-imported French word list (lib/text/word-list.ts, dynamically imported on first entry into the racing phase so it never bloats other pages' bundles), pre-normalized into a Set<string> keyed by normalizeWord() output for O(1) case/accent-insensitive lookup. MUST be sourced from a permissively-licensed dataset (this repo is public AND is the prod infra per project convention — same licensing bar as the sticker-sourcing work already done in docs/STICKER-SOURCING.md) before this game ships; flag this explicitly as a build prerequisite to confirm with the author, not an implementation detail to gloss over.
specs.turnModel: No turn gating anywhere during the racing phase — this is the whole point of the mechanic, and it's a deliberate response to the two turn-gating bugs already found twice in this app (Doodle Duel's missing "duel-next-round" message, Word Sonar's turn-gated-guess UX bug). The only "turn"-shaped thing in this game is the start/end role assignment, which is a per-round LABEL (who picks which letter), not a gate on any ACTION — both players pick their letter simultaneously with zero dependency on the other, and both players submit racing guesses simultaneously with zero dependency on the other. Nothing in this game ever makes one player wait for the other's move before their own becomes valid, except waiting for the round's adjudicator's verdict message (see singleAuthority) — which is a resolution-of-an-already-completed-race step, not a "wait for your turn" gate.
specs.singleAuthority:
Per-round adjudicator, rotating by the same deterministic parity as the start/end role assignment (adjudicatorIsInitiator(round) = round % 2 === 0 — reuse the exact same parity function so there's only one source of truth for "whose turn is it to hold authority this round," never two independently-computed parities that could drift apart). The adjudicator is the ONLY device that ever emits edgeletters-round-result; the non-adjudicating player's client never declares a local win from its own "I typed first" feeling — it submits its claim and then WAITS for edgeletters-round-result before showing any outcome, exactly like Doodle Duel's drawer being the sole judge of guesses transplanted onto a race instead of a fixed role.

Why the other side can't cheat or desync: the adjudicator resolves ordering purely from events arriving in ITS OWN single-threaded message queue — its own claim-ready moment and the peer's edgeletters-claim message are both just events in one linear timeline on one device, so "which happened first" is unambiguous there even though it would be genuinely ambiguous if both peers tried to compare their own local clocks (no synced clock is trusted for this, unlike the photo capture's clock-sync which exists for a different purpose). Before crediting EITHER claim (its own or the peer's) as the winner, the adjudicator independently re-validates the claimed word against the shared bundled word list + that round's start/end letters using the exact same isValidWord() the submitter already ran locally — so a modified or buggy client claiming a garbage "winning" word is simply not credited. This is safe specifically because the word list is static bundled data identical in every build, never something one peer tells the other about — no trust is ever extended over the network for what counts as a valid word.
messageTypes: { t: "edgeletters-start" } — sent once by the host on "Lancer la partie"; carries no config (nothing to choose, unlike Word Sonar's word-length picker) — just resets both clients to round 0 / phase "picking".

{ t: "edgeletters-letter-pick"; round: number; role: "start" | "end"; letter: string } — sent by each player the instant they lock in a letter (or the instant their own pickDurationMs soft timer auto-picks one for them). `role` is included explicitly rather than re-derived from round parity on receipt, so a parity-computation drift between clients (extremely unlikely, but a real bug class already seen with drawerIsInitiatorForRound-style logic) can never cause the receiver to file the letter into the wrong slot.

{ t: "edgeletters-claim"; round: number; word: string } — sent by a client the moment its own local validation (word list + start/end letter + min length) passes; the client locks itself out from further submissions this round immediately after sending.

{ t: "edgeletters-round-result"; round: number; winner: "host" | "guest" | null; word: string | null } — emitted ONLY by that round's adjudicator (rotates by round parity, see singleAuthority), after independently re-validating whichever claim it resolves as first. `winner: null` / `word: null` is the draw case, emitted by the adjudicator on its own local raceDurationMs expiry if no valid claim arrived in time. BOTH clients (including the adjudicator itself) treat this message, not their own local guess about who was first, as authoritative for the scoreboard.

{ t: "edgeletters-race-timeout"; round: number } — a client sends this the instant its own local raceDurationMs timer (started symmetrically for both sides on entering "racing") expires with no claim sent yet; guarded by the same round-tagged idempotency the adjudicator already applies to edgeletters-round-result, so if both sides' timers fire within milliseconds of each other only one draw resolution is ever applied.

{ t: "edgeletters-advance"; round: number } — first player to click "Manche suivante"/"Voir le récap" after a reveal sends this; both sides guard with an advancedRef exactly like duel-next-round/mindmatch-advance/wordsonar-advance, to avoid the exact double-advance desync bug already found twice in this codebase.
syncPitfalls: Race-resolution ambiguity: two peers can submit valid claims within milliseconds of each other over an unordered-relative-to-each-other pair of send directions. Fixed by giving ONE rotating adjudicator per round sole authority to declare the winner from its own single-threaded message-arrival order — never by comparing local clocks or trusting either peer's self-reported "I was first."

Turn-gating a race is the exact mistake already made twice in this app (Word Sonar's originally turn-gated guess, and the general lesson from Doodle Duel's missing advance message) — Edge Letters has zero turn concept during racing by design, so this bug class structurally cannot recur here.

Simultaneous symmetric timeout: unlike Word Sonar's turn timer (owned by whoever currently holds the turn, so only one side ever has an active deadline), Edge Letters' race timer starts identically on BOTH sides at the same phase transition — so both could independently fire edgeletters-race-timeout near-simultaneously. Guarded with the same round-tagged idempotency pattern already used for the advance message, so only the first-processed timeout is ever applied regardless of which side's timer fired first.

Never trust a claimed word over the network: the adjudicator re-runs the exact same local isValidWord() check against the shared bundled word list before crediting ANY claim, including its own — safe only because the word list is static build-time data identical on both devices, not something a peer asserts about itself.

Closure/ref staleness: the data channel listener is mounted once (`useEffect` dep `[dataChannel]`), so round index, both letters, the adjudicator's own pending claim state, and the advance/timeout idempotency guards must all be read through refs kept current by dedicated effects — never closed-over state, following the exact same discipline already documented (and the exact bug already found) in use-duel-session.ts and use-word-sonar-session.ts.

Role assignment sent explicitly rather than re-derived: edgeletters-letter-pick carries `role` in the payload instead of making the receiver recompute round parity to decide whether an incoming letter is the start or end letter — removes an entire class of "the two sides silently disagree about whose turn/role this is" bug before it can exist, at the cost of a few extra bytes per message.

Peer disconnect mid-race or mid-adjudication: reuse the room-level connection status machinery already built for the photobooth (RTCPeerConnectionState-derived reconnecting/disconnected handling) rather than inventing new detection — on data channel loss, invalidate the in-flight round exactly like a half-captured pose is invalidated in use-capture-session.ts, and on the `hello` reconnection handshake, have the round's adjudicator resend the last-known edgeletters-round-result if the round had already resolved, or restart the round from "picking" if it hadn't — never rely on RTCDataChannel.onopen alone, for the same proven reason documented in this app's reconnect handling.
specs.uiNotes: Follows the established mini-game screen shape: dark-on-result / generic no-prénom lobby, a "Comment ça marche" rules block on first entry (mandatory per the lesson learned from Doodle Duel shipping without one), FaceBubbles.tsx (already generalized across Doodle Duel/Mind Match) reused unchanged for the persistent camera/mic presence during play. Picking phase: a single full-width A-Z tile grid, big role header above it ("Choisis la lettre de DÉBUT" in coral / "Choisis la lettre de FIN" — reuse the app's existing convention that coral marks the primary/host-adjacent action and violet is reserved specifically for the "join" path, never used decoratively elsewhere per the Doodle Duel gradient-color fix). Racing phase: the two locked letters rendered large and fixed at the top ("○ ⟨X⟩ … ⟨Y⟩ ○"), a single text input with live inline validation (not-a-real-word / doesn't-match-the-letters micro-copy, subtle shake/red-border feedback rather than a blocking modal — never alert()/confirm()), submit disabled the instant this client's own claim is sent (visually: input replaced by a "En attente du résultat…" state) so the player never wonders if their tap registered. Reveal: winning word large and centered, small checkmark badge on the winner's side, running score persists in a fixed header across rounds (mirrors Doodle Duel/Word Sonar's score header). Recap: canvas-composed card, one row per round (round #, the two letters, the winning word or "Manche nulle", who won), score in the header, brand footer — composed and downloaded/shared via the already-extracted lib/share-or-download.ts helper, same as Doodle Duel's and Word Sonar's recap cards, so no new sharing code is needed.

specs.name: Fleet Siege
specs.rules:
Grid: 8×8 for both players (config.fleetSiege.gridSize = 8), centralized in shared game config so both clients always agree on legal coordinates without ever exchanging grid dimensions. Fleet: 3 ships per player, sizes [4, 3, 2] (config.fleetSiege.shipSizes) — deliberately smaller than classic 10x10/5-ship Battleship to keep matches short, consistent with Doodle Duel/Word Sonar/Mind Match's quick-session positioning.

Phase 1 — Placement (private, client-side only): each player places their 3 ships on their own grid, straight lines only (horizontal or vertical), fully in-bounds, no overlapping cells between ships. No adjacency restriction (ships may touch) — kept simple, no cross-checking possible or needed since the peer never sees the layout at all. A "Randomize" button is allowed and is NOT the kind of shared randomness the architecture worries about: it only ever decides that player's own secret data, exactly like each Word Sonar player privately choosing their own secret word — no trust or synchronization required because nothing about it is ever compared against or revealed to the peer at placement time.

Phase 2 — Battle: turns strictly alternate, host fires first. Turn order is derived, never negotiated: shotIndex 0, 2, 4… belong to the host; 1, 3, 5… to the guest (identical parity logic to Doodle Duel's drawerIsInitiatorForRound, and to Word Sonar's ask-alternation) — both sides compute "whose turn" identically and locally, no network message dedicated to turn-passing exists because the ordered/reliable data channel guarantees fire→result round-trips arrive in the order sent, and the next turn's legality falls straight out of that count. The attacker picks an unfired coordinate on the opponent's fogged grid; the defender (fleet owner) computes hit/miss from their own locally-held board and replies. A ship is sunk when all its cells have been hit; the fleet owner declares gameOver the instant their own last ship is sunk. Win condition: first side whose full fleet is sunk loses.

Phase 3 — Reveal & rematch: once gameOver is true (computed independently and identically on each side from the same fire/result stream), both clients broadcast their full board so the loser's (and winner's) actual ship placements are shown side by side on the result screen — this is the only point ship layouts are ever transmitted, and it is purely cosmetic (game is already decided). Either player can click "Play again"; this resets both sides to a fresh Placement phase on the same connection, no reload, no WebRTC renegotiation, alternating who fires first on each successive match (match 0 → host first, match 1 → guest first, etc., computed locally from a shared match counter, not networked separately).
specs.turnModel: Strictly alternating exclusive turns — this is the one mechanic in the games-hub lineup where turn-gating is actually correct, because (per the constraint list) each shot's value genuinely depends on reading the opponent's prior results; there is no "already-known answer" to blurt out early the way Word Sonar's full-word guess was. Turn ownership is never sent as its own message — it is derived purely from shotIndex parity plus the immutable host/guest role, exactly like Doodle Duel's per-round drawer parity. Because the data channel is ordered and reliable, a fire/fire-result pair always completes before the next fire can be sent, so both peers' local "whose turn" computation can never disagree without a channel-level fault (out of scope, same as every other game here). The receiving (defending) side additionally validates that an incoming siege-fire's shotIndex matches the parity it expects before evaluating it, and silently ignores anything else — cheap defense against a stray/duplicate message, not a trust mechanism (see singleAuthority).
specs.singleAuthority: Direct extension of Word Sonar's "owner computes the answer locally" pattern, applied spatially instead of lexically: each player's own placed fleet is the sole source of truth for their own board, and it is NEVER serialized or sent while the game is live — only the verdict (hit/miss/sunk/game-over) computed from it crosses the wire, in direct reply to a specific incoming shot. There is no separate "referee" peer and no shared board state to keep consistent, so there is nothing to desync on the placement side at all — the entire attack surface collapses to "does the fleet owner report truthfully," which is the same accepted trust boundary Word Sonar already lives with for its letter-owner, not a new one Fleet Siege introduces. The only other authority question — who fires first, and who fires first on each rematch — is resolved without any negotiation or randomness: host-first, alternating by a locally-computed match counter, identical on both sides by construction (same category of trick as Doodle Duel's round-parity drawer assignment), so there is no dice roll or coin flip to fight over and no need for either side to prove fairness to the other.
messageTypes: siege-ready: {} — sent once when a player finishes and confirms fleet placement; each side tracks localReady and peerReady independently and transitions to Battle only when both are true, order of arrival irrelevant (a boolean AND, not a toggle, so it's naturally idempotent against being received more than once)

siege-fire: { row: number, col: number, shotIndex: number } — attacker's shot at a coordinate on the opponent's board; shotIndex is the shared, locally-derived turn counter, included so the receiver can verify turn legality and reject anything out of parity

siege-fire-result: { row: number, col: number, shotIndex: number, result: 'hit' | 'miss', sunkShip?: { id: string, cells: { row: number, col: number }[] }, gameOver: boolean } — sent by the fleet owner in direct reply to siege-fire, computed entirely from their own board; sunkShip is present only on the exact shot that completes a ship and carries just that ship's cells (never the rest of the board) so the attacker's UI can lift the fog on only that ship; gameOver:true is set by the fleet owner themselves the instant their own last ship is sunk — no separate end-of-game message that could race against the last fire-result

siege-reveal-board: { ships: { id: string, cells: { row: number, col: number }[] }[] } — sent by each side once gameOver is locally true (both winner and loser send it symmetrically); the only message in the protocol that ever exposes a full board, and only after the outcome is already decided, purely for the result screen's side-by-side reveal

siege-rematch: {} — sent by whichever player clicks 'Play again' first; guarded locally by a rematchRequestedRef exactly like duel-next-round/mindmatch-advance so a near-simultaneous double-click from both screens doesn't double-fire; on send or receipt both sides clear their boards, increment the shared match counter, and return to Placement with first-shooter swapped
syncPitfalls: Never start Battle for only one side: siege-ready is tracked as an independent flag per side and the transition requires the AND of both, not 'I sent mine so I'll start' — avoids a Doodle-Duel-style 'started before the other side was actually ready' class of bug even though the failure mode here (one player's board not truly locked in) is milder than a live countdown.

Turn order is derived from shotIndex parity, never sent as its own 'now it's your turn' message — this sidesteps an entire class of desync risk (a dedicated turn-pass message getting dropped or duplicated would leave the two sides disagreeing about whose turn it is); parity is recomputed identically from data both sides already have, so there's nothing extra to lose in transit.

Defending side validates incoming siege-fire's shotIndex against the parity it expects and silently ignores mismatches, rather than trusting every incoming fire blindly — cheap insurance against a stray duplicate or an out-of-order client bug, same spirit as Word Sonar's inherent local-computation trust but applied defensively at the message boundary too.

Rematch uses the exact same idempotency-guard lesson learned twice already (Doodle Duel's duel-next-round, Mind Match's mindmatch-advance): any state transition both sides must agree on gets a network message plus a ref-guard against double-firing, never an assumption that 'my own click is enough, I'll just reset locally' — a bare local reset was precisely the bug that broke Doodle Duel's round advancement.

Fleet layout is never transmitted while the game is live, only the per-shot verdict and, on a sunk ship, just that ship's own cells — deliberately narrower than Doodle Duel's live-stroke-streaming or Mind Match's word exchange, because here the private data (the whole board) is far more valuable to leak early than a single word guess would be; the full-board siege-reveal-board message is delayed until gameOver is already true on both sides specifically so this never doubles as a mid-game information leak.

Grid size and fleet ship sizes live only in shared config (never negotiated or sent), so both clients always agree on which coordinates and ship lengths are legal without a single round-trip — mirrors the existing rule that algorithm/product constants belong in config.ts, not exchanged over the wire.
specs.uiNotes: Two grids per screen during Battle: "Your Fleet" (own 8×8 board, ships always visible to their owner, incoming hit/miss markers overlaid as they arrive) and "Target Waters" (opponent's board under fog of war — only cells you've fired at show a hit/miss marker, and a sunk ship's siege-fire-result reveals exactly that ship's cells as a small ship-outline overlay, not a full-board reveal). Turn banner above the target grid: "Your turn — fire!" vs "Waiting for Partenaire" derived from the same local parity computation used for message validation, with the target grid's cells disabled (not just visually muted) whenever it isn't the local player's turn, and already-fired cells disabled permanently regardless of turn. Placement phase: tap-to-select a ship from a small fleet tray, tap-to-place, tap again (or a rotate icon) to toggle orientation, with a "Randomize" shortcut and a "Confirm fleet" button that sends siege-ready and locks the board from further edits. FaceBubbles (components/room/FaceBubbles.tsx, already shared between Doodle Duel and Mind Match) stays visible through both phases, generic "Toi"/"Partenaire" labels, no prénom capture — same scope choice already made for both existing games. Game-over screen: both boards fully revealed side by side (from siege-reveal-board) with a win/lose banner and a "Rejouer" button; visual language follows the established coral gradient for the game's own promo/CTA surfaces (violet stays reserved exclusively for the "join" path per existing convention). Routes: /fleet-siege, /fleet-siege/join, /fleet-siege/r/[code], root component FleetSiegeClient.tsx, hook use-fleet-siege-session.ts, types/fleetsiege-realtime.ts, board/placement logic under lib/fleet-siege/ (board.ts for hit/sunk computation, placement.ts for overlap/bounds validation) — new entry added to lib/games/registry.ts for its room-code prefix and landing promo copy, alongside Doodle Duel and Mind Match. E2E coverage (e2e/tests/fleet-siege.spec.ts) should mirror the existing suites: both sides place fleets, alternate shots to a full sink, verify the reveal screen shows correct ship layouts, then verify a single-sided "Rejouer" click resets both screens to Placement with the first-shooter swapped.

specs.name: Duo Quiz
specs.rules:
Two peers answer identical static trivia questions from a JSON bank shipped identically in both app bundles (lib/duo-quiz/question-bank.json — array of {id, prompt, choices[4], correctIndex, category?}). A session is config.duoQuiz.rounds questions (default 8), each with a fixed answer window config.duoQuiz.roundDurationMs (default 15000ms, deliberately snappier than Doodle Duel's 60s — trivia recall is fast, unlike drawing).

Per round: the round authority (see singleAuthority) broadcasts the question's full prompt/choices and a duration. Both peers see it at the same instant and answer immediately and independently — no turn order, no waiting. Selecting a choice locks it in (further taps disabled), grades it locally against the peer's own copy of the bank by questionId, and sends only the boolean verdict over the wire — the correct answer itself is never transmitted as new information, since both clients already hold it in their identical static bundle.

A round ends the moment BOTH verdicts are known (whichever answers second triggers early end — snappier than waiting out the full timer) or when the timer elapses, whichever comes first; unanswered-at-deadline counts as incorrect. The round-end reveal (correct choice highlighted green, own wrong pick red if applicable) is gated on an authority-sent message, never computed independently on each side, so the two screens can't reveal at visibly different moments. After a short reveal pause (config.duoQuiz.revealPauseMs, ~1.5s) the authority advances to the next round, or to game-over after the last one. Score is 1 point per correct answer; no speed bonus in v1 (documented as a possible later enhancement, not required now). Recap screen shows one row per round (question + correct/incorrect for each side) plus final tally, downloadable/shareable like Doodle Duel's and Mind Match's recaps via the shared lib/share-or-download.ts helper and a new lib/duo-quiz/compose-recap.ts canvas composer. Replay resets both sides to round 0 locally on the same connection, no renegotiation, no network message — same pattern as Doodle Duel/Mind Match replay().

Room code prefix: add "Q" (Duo Quiz) to ROOM_KIND_PREFIX in lib/room-code.ts / lib/games/registry.ts (P=photo, D=duel, M=mindmatch already taken). Routes: /duoquiz, /duoquiz/join, /duoquiz/r/[code], root component DuoQuizClient.tsx, no participant-name capture (generic "Toi"/"Partenaire" labels, same scope decision as Doodle Duel and Mind Match — the hello/config name handshake is photo-specific and not worth duplicating here).

Known accepted trust boundary (documented, not a bug to fix): since the full question bank is static client-side data, a devtools-savvy player could in principle inspect it to see answers in advance — this is inherent to the "no server, no secret backend" architecture (same class of trade-off as other P2P design decisions already accepted in this codebase) and is not solvable without a server, which is explicitly out of scope.
specs.turnModel: Fully non-turn-gated within a round: the instant duo-quiz-round-start arrives, both peers can answer immediately and independently — neither waits for the other to move first (same principle as Word Sonar's non-turn-gated full-word guess, and explicitly the opposite of Doodle Duel's alternating drawer/guesser split, because nothing here is asymmetric-information that would make simultaneous action unfair). The only sequencing in the whole game is across rounds, not within one: round N+1 cannot begin until round N has been graded (both verdicts known or timer elapsed) and revealed — that gating is authority/timer-driven, never a manual "ready" click from either human, and is not a "turn" in the alternating sense, just a round boundary.
specs.singleAuthority: The room initiator (host) is the sole round authority for the ENTIRE session — it never alternates, unlike Doodle Duel's per-round drawer swap, because no side of Duo Quiz ever holds privileged information the other lacks: the question bank, the choices, and the correct answers are identical static data already present in both bundles before the game even starts. Concretely, the host alone: (1) locally shuffles round order via Fisher-Yates over the shared bank at game start (never transmitted — the peer never needs to reproduce or verify this shuffle), (2) broadcasts each round's question content and answer-window duration, (3) runs the one authoritative round timer and decides when a round ends (both verdicts in, or timer elapsed) and when the reveal happens, and (4) sends the idempotency-guarded advance to the next round or the final game-over message. The guest does not need to trust the host's shuffle for fairness in any adversarial sense — both players see the identical prompt at the identical instant with zero lead-time advantage, and each grades its own answer from its own local copy of the same public bank — so the host's only real "power" is cosmetic round ORDERING across the session, never an information or scoring asymmetry within a single round. This is a deliberately simpler trust model than Doodle Duel's (where the drawer must keep a secret word hidden) precisely because Duo Quiz has no secret to protect.
messageTypes: duo-quiz-round-start { roundIndex: number; totalRounds: number; questionId: string; prompt: string; choices: string[]; durationMs: number } — sent only by the authority; choices/prompt are sent verbatim (not just questionId) so both sides render identical text even if bundle content ever drifted; durationMs seeds the guest's own local countdown tick.

duo-quiz-answer-result { roundIndex: number; correct: boolean; answeredAt: "in-time" | "timeout" } — sent by EITHER peer the instant it grades its own locked-in choice (or is auto-marked timeout); never carries which specific choice was picked, only the verdict, since only true/false is needed for the scoreboard and the correct answer is never new information over the wire.

duo-quiz-round-end { roundIndex: number; correctIndex: number } — sent only by the authority once both verdicts are known or the timer elapses; this is a synchronization BEACON, not new information (both sides can already look up correctIndex locally via questionId) — its sole job is making sure both screens reveal at the same instant instead of racing to their own local reveal.

duo-quiz-game-over { hostScore: number; guestScore: number } — sent only by the authority in place of the next round-start once totalRounds is reached; acts as a failsafe canonical tally in case a single answer-result was ever lost in transit, so the recap can't show two different final scores on the two screens.
syncPitfalls: Frozen guest countdown: the non-authority side must start its own local tick from the received durationMs the moment duo-quiz-round-start arrives (same pattern already used for Word Sonar/Doodle Duel's non-authority timer) — without it, the guest's countdown UI would sit frozen at its starting value for the whole round.

Double round-advance: because early-end (both answered) and timer-expiry (deadline hit) are two independent local triggers that could both fire in the authority's own client, guard advancement with a single ref (roundAdvancedRef) checked-and-set atomically before sending duo-quiz-round-end/next round-start — otherwise the authority could send two round-starts for what should be one round, skipping a question. This is the same bug CLASS as Doodle Duel's duel-next-round and Mind Match's mindmatch-advance double-click bugs, just raced by two local conditions on one client instead of two humans clicking on two screens.

Reveal-order desync: if either side computed and displayed the correct answer purely from its own local timer/local bank lookup instead of waiting for duo-quiz-round-end, one player could see the answer flash while their partner is still actively choosing — feels broken and spoils the round. Fix: the correct-answer highlight is only ever rendered after the authority-sent round-end message is received, never on a local-only timeout on the non-authority side.

Stale closure over round state: the data-channel message listener is attached once in an effect with a narrow dependency array ([dataChannel]); anything it reads to grade or track state (current roundIndex, current questionId/correctIndex, accumulated scores) must be read through refs kept current by dedicated effects, not through captured component state — otherwise the listener keeps judging every future round against round 0 forever, exactly the closure bug already found and fixed in use-duel-session.ts and use-mindmatch-session.ts.

Late/duplicate answer-result after the round already advanced: every incoming duo-quiz-answer-result and duo-quiz-round-end must be checked against the roundIndex currently being tracked and discarded if it doesn't match, so a message delayed by network jitter can't retroactively flip a score or double-count a verdict after the local state has already moved on to the next round.

No runtime bank-version negotiation: correctness relies on both clients being on the same deployed build of the static question bank (same assumption already accepted for e.g. the frame registry) — Duo Quiz avoids the risk mostly by sending full prompt/choices text over the wire rather than trusting the peer's local copy to match, but correctIndex grading still assumes matching bundles; this is a deployment-practice guarantee, not a runtime protocol, and should be called out explicitly rather than silently assumed.

Routes app/[locale]/duoquiz/{page.tsx, join/page.tsx, r/[code]/page.tsx}, root DuoQuizClient.tsx, hook hooks/use-duo-quiz-session.ts, types types/duo-quiz-realtime.ts, bank+helpers lib/duo-quiz/{question-bank.json, pick-questions.ts, compose-recap.ts}, components components/duoquiz/{DuoQuizLobby.tsx, DuoQuizRound.tsx, DuoQuizRecap.tsx}. No name/config capture, generic "Toi"/"Partenaire" labels throughout, same scope decision as Doodle Duel and Mind Match.

Prompt text large and centered, 4 choice buttons in a 2x2 grid (rounded-16-18px per design system, never rounded-full except chips), a countdown bar/ring ticking down from durationMs. Tapping a choice locks it immediately (buttons disabled, chosen one gets a subtle selected state) — no "submit" step, no waiting-for-partner blocking overlay beyond a small unobtrusive "partenaire répond…" microstate. On duo-quiz-round-end: correct choice turns green, own incorrect pick (if any) turns red, small scoreboard tick animates (+1) via Framer Motion, sober per project convention (150–300ms ease-out).
