Rejouer button resets to round 0 locally on the same connection, no renegotiation, matching Doodle Duel/Mind Match replay().

All visible strings added to messages/{fr,en}.ts under a new duoQuiz namespace — never inline in components, per project i18n convention. e2e coverage: e2e/tests/duo-quiz.spec.ts — full game (all rounds), an early-both-answered round vs a timeout round, reveal-sync check (no flash-before-partner-answers), recap download, and replay without reconnecting.

specs.name: Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe
specs.turnModel: Strict alternating exclusive turns — the one case among these games where full turn-gating is correct, because every move's legality is a direct function of the immediately preceding move (which sub-board is "active"). Symbol/first-mover assignment is resolved with zero network messages: host (isInitiator) is always X and always moves first; guest is always O — same deterministic-by-connection-role convention as Doodle Duel's `drawerIsInitiatorForRound`, never re-negotiated, never sent over the wire. Whose turn it is is never itself transmitted — both sides derive it as `moveLog.length % 2 === 0 ? "X" : "O"` from the shared append-only move log, so it can never disagree between peers as long as the move log itself is in sync (see syncPitfalls for how that's guaranteed). A client only allows local pointer input on a cell when TWO independently-computed conditions both hold: (1) locally-derived turn === my symbol, and (2) the clicked (boardIndex, cellIndex) is inside the legal-move set for the current state (see singleAuthority). There is no separate "ask" vs "guess" split like Word Sonar — every action is the same shape (place a mark) and always waits its turn, because unlike Word Sonar's full-word guess, there is no case here where the responder already privately knows the answer and forcing them to wait would be bad UX — a move genuinely cannot be evaluated before the opponent's prior move exists.
specs.singleAuthority: No shared randomness is needed anywhere in this game (fully deterministic from the move log), so there is no RNG-authority question the way Bingo would have one. The only two things that need a "who decides" answer: (1) first-mover/symbol assignment — resolved locally and identically by both sides from the pre-existing `isInitiator` boolean already available from useRoomConnection, exactly like Doodle Duel's drawer parity, never transmitted; (2) move legality and win/draw detection — NOT owned by either peer individually. Both run the exact same pure, deterministic functions (`isLegalMove(state, boardIndex, cellIndex)`, `checkSubBoardResult(cells)`, `checkMetaResult(subBoardResults)`, `activeBoard(state)`) independently against their own copy of the shared move log, imported from one shared module (`lib/uttt/win-check.ts`) so there is exactly one implementation of each rule, not a sender's copy and a receiver's copy that could quietly drift apart. Each side IS the sole authority over gating its own local player's input (disabling illegal cells before a click can even happen), but neither side is authoritative over the other's move — the receiving side re-validates every incoming `uttt-move` against its own independently-computed legal-move set purely as a defensive corruption check (catches a client bug, e.g. an off-by-one in the boardIndex↔cellIndex mapping), not as anti-cheat: the trust model here is the same as every other SnapLover game (two consenting remote friends), not an adversarial one, so there's no need to hide state from either player — the entire board is public knowledge to both the instant it changes, which is the key structural difference from Doodle Duel (secret word) and Word Sonar (secret word) that makes this game simpler to keep in sync despite its more elaborate rules.
specs.rules:
Board model: a 3x3 meta-board of nine 3x3 sub-boards. Sub-boards and cells within a sub-board are both indexed 0-8 in row-major order (0 1 2 / 3 4 5 / 6 7 8). Cell state: null | "X" | "O". Sub-board state: "open" | "won-x" | "won-o" | "draw" (draw = all 9 cells filled, no 3-in-a-row). A sub-board's state is computed once from its 9 cells via the standard 8 win-lines (3 rows, 3 cols, 2 diagonals); once decided (won or draw) it is permanently locked — no further marks can be placed in it regardless of the active-board rule below.

Move legality (`isLegalMove`): a move at (boardIndex, cellIndex) is legal iff — the cell is empty AND boardIndex's sub-board is not yet decided AND boardIndex matches the current "active board" constraint. Active-board constraint: on the very first move of the game there is no constraint (any open cell in any board is legal — represented as activeBoard = null, meaning "any"). After every move, the active board for the opponent's NEXT move is forced to equal the cellIndex just played (the position within the local 3x3 board maps directly to which of the 9 sub-boards must be played next) — UNLESS that target sub-board is already decided (won or draw), in which case the constraint lifts entirely and the opponent may play in ANY still-open sub-board (activeBoard becomes null again for that turn only).

Meta win/draw: the meta-board is evaluated with the exact same 8-line check, treating "won-x"/"won-o" sub-board states as X-claimed/O-claimed cells and "open"/"draw" as unclaimed. Three sub-boards claimed by the same player in a line ends the game immediately as a win for that player, even if other sub-boards are still open (an in-progress sub-board is simply abandoned — no more moves are ever routed into it since the game is already over). If all 9 sub-boards reach "won-x"/"won-o"/"draw" with no 3-in-a-row on the meta-board, the game ends in a full draw.

Symbol/turn order: host = X, moves first; guest = O. Never renegotiated mid-game, never sent over the network (see singleAuthority).
messageTypes: uttt-ready — { t: "uttt-ready" }, no payload. Sent once by each side the instant its message listener effect mounts. Input stays disabled on BOTH sides (even for host/X) until each has both sent its own uttt-ready and received the peer's — this is the exact same 'proof the partner is actually listening' gate the project already documents needing for the hello/config handshake and the reconnect fix (relying on dataChannel.onopen/readyState alone does not guarantee the OTHER side's listener is attached yet, so a message dispatched before that can be silently lost).

uttt-move — { t: "uttt-move"; boardIndex: number (0-8); cellIndex: number (0-8); moveIndex: number }. The only gameplay message. moveIndex is the position this move occupies in the sender's own move log at send time (i.e. moveLog.length just before appending) — carried purely as an idempotency/ordering guard per this codebase's established convention (same role as the guards on duel-next-round/mindmatch-advance), not because the WebRTC data channel (ordered:true, reliable) is expected to reorder or duplicate in practice. Sender applies the move to local state optimistically at send time (no round-trip wait, needed for responsive feel) using the shared isLegalMove() gate; receiver validates moveIndex === its own moveLogRef.current.length AND re-runs isLegalMove() before applying — either check failing means drop the message and treat it as a bug to investigate, never silently 'fix up' or resync from thin air (there is no server truth to resync against).

uttt-rematch — { t: "uttt-rematch" }, no payload. Sent by whichever side clicks 'Rejouer' first after the game ends (win or draw), guarded by a local ref (rematchArmedRef) so if both sides click at nearly the same moment only one reset actually fires per game — same idempotency-guard lesson already applied twice before (Doodle Duel's duel-next-round, Mind Match's mindmatch-advance). Resets moveLog to empty on both sides; host stays X, guest stays O (unchanged across rematches — mirrors Mind Match's replay(), no renegotiation).
syncPitfalls: Listener-not-yet-attached race: if the host (X, moves first) sends its opening uttt-move the instant the data channel opens, but the guest's message-handler effect hasn't finished mounting yet, that first move is lost forever (a 'message' event fired before addEventListener is attached is simply never delivered) — this is the same root cause already documented for the photo flow's hello/config race and the reconnect race. Fixed structurally here by gating ALL input (including the host's very first move) behind the uttt-ready handshake rather than behind dataChannel.onopen/readyState.

Sender/receiver legality drift: the sender pre-checks a move is legal before sending it, and the receiver checks it again after receiving it — if these were two independently hand-written copies of the same rule (e.g. one forgets that a 'draw' sub-board, not just a 'won' one, also lifts the active-board constraint), the two boards silently diverge, and because there is no server to reconcile against, every subsequent move compounds the divergence until the game is unrecoverable. Avoided by importing one single isLegalMove()/activeBoard() implementation from lib/uttt/win-check.ts on both the send-gate call site and the receive-validate call site — never two copies of the same rule.

Stale-closure bug (recurring pattern in every session hook in this codebase): the data channel's onmessage listener is attached once, in an effect with a narrow dependency array (typically just [dataChannel]), so anything the handler reads — the move log, the derived active board, whose turn it is — must be read through a ref kept fresh by a separate effect, never read directly off React state captured in that closure, or it reproduces the exact bug already found and fixed in use-capture-session.ts and use-duel-session.ts (values frozen at mount, never updated after the first move/round).

Rematch desync: if 'Rejouer' only reset state locally with no network message, one player could click it and see a fresh empty board while their partner is still staring at the finished/won-board overlay with their own unclicked 'Rejouer' button — the same class of bug as Doodle Duel's real 'duel-next-round' desync (discovered live: one screen said round 2/3, the other 3/3, same game). Avoided here by sending uttt-rematch on first click, gated by a local idempotency ref against a double-fire if both sides click within the same round trip.

Active-board derivation computed differently on the two sides: 'which sub-board(s) are currently playable' is derived state, never transmitted on the wire, so any subtle disagreement in how each side computes it (an off-by-one in the cellIndex→boardIndex mapping, or forgetting that a full-but-undecided... — actually a sub-board is always decided once full, so specifically forgetting that BOTH 'won' and 'draw' free the constraint, not just 'won') makes the two clients highlight a different set of legal cells, so a move one side considers legal the other will reject on receipt. This is the single highest-risk piece of genuinely novel logic in this game (per the build-priority rationale), so activeBoard()/isLegalMove() should get direct unit tests against hand-constructed board states, not just relying on the e2e happy-path spec to exercise every corner case (forced-into-decided-board, forced-into-full-board, first move, meta win before all sub-boards decided).
specs.uiNotes: Layout: a 3x3 CSS grid of nine 3x3 CSS grids (nested grid-in-grid), same responsive mobile-first approach as PhotoStrip's canvas-preview sizing — the whole meta-board scales as one square unit and should stay legible down to a single mobile column width. The single currently-legal sub-board (or all open sub-boards, during a free-move turn) gets a visible highlight (ring/glow in --coral, matching the existing 'primary action' color per the design system) while every other sub-board's cells are visually dimmed and unclickable — this IS the core piece of UI feedback the whole game hinges on, more important than any animation. A decided sub-board stops showing its individual cell marks as the focal element and instead stamps one large X/O (or a tie glyph) across that whole sub-board, exactly like physical Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe play — reinforces at a glance which of the 9 boards are still live. Turn indicator: reuse the existing generalized components/room/FaceBubbles.tsx with the same generic 'Toi'/'Partenaire' labels already used by Doodle Duel and Mind Match (no prénoms, no config screen — /uttt should be the simplest lobby of the three games: a single 'Créer une partie' button, nothing to configure, matching the 'no config to agree on' framing already used for Mind Match). Mark placement gets a small, sober Framer Motion scale/fade-in (150-300ms ease-out, per project convention — no gadget animation); a sub-board being won gets a slightly more pronounced stamp animation; the meta-board win gets a full-board highlight overlay, deliberately NOT confetti/particles (out of step with the rest of the app's restrained motion language). Recap/share: unlike Doodle Duel and Mind Match, this is one continuous game rather than N repeated rounds, so there's no multi-row recap card — the shareable artifact is a single composed canvas of the final 9-board grid plus a winner/draw banner and the standard brand footer, reusing the existing lib/share-or-download.ts helper (same extraction point already used by Doodle Duel's and Mind Match's recaps) rather than inventing a new share path. Registry: add one entry to lib/games/registry.ts — kind "uttt", prefix "U" (confirmed free against existing P/D/W/M), roomPath "/uttt/r", joinPath "/uttt/join", createPath "/uttt", name "Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe", new icon (e.g. lucide Grid3x3), promoNamespace "landing.uttt" — everything else (code-prefix collision guard, InlineJoinField dispatch, robots.ts exclusion) falls out of that registry automatically, per the registry's own design intent. Landing promotion should slot into whatever unified 'Jeux' hub block gets built (already an open TODO in this codebase for Mind Match) rather than adding a third bespoke full-width promo section. Suggested new files, following the exact naming pattern of the two existing games: types/uttt.ts (board/cell/sub-board state shapes), types/uttt-realtime.ts (the three message types above), lib/uttt/win-check.ts (the shared pure legality/win functions), hooks/use-uttt-session.ts, components/uttt/{UtttClient,UtttLobby,UtttBoard,UtttRecap}.tsx, app/[locale]/uttt/{page.tsx, join/page.tsx, r/[code]/page.tsx}, e2e/tests/uttt.spec.ts (full game to a meta-win, a forced-into-decided-board free move, and a rematch, at minimum).

specs.name: Copy Cat
specs.turnModel: Not turn-gated in the alternating-message sense at all — within a round there is exactly one linear handoff, never a back-and-forth. Round flow: (1) Poser is the only one who can act — they see their own live camera, no chrono, no prep countdown, and press a manual "Capture" button whenever they're ready (deliberately unlimited think time — Copy Cat needs zero time pressure to work as a mechanic, unlike Doodle Duel's chrono). (2) Mimic is fully passive/blocked until the reference photo has FULLY arrived (gated on the img-end message, not img-meta — see pitfalls). Nothing the Mimic could click before that would do anything, so this isn't "turn-gating for convenience," it's a real data dependency. (3) Once the reference lands, the Mimic becomes the only one who can act — ghost-overlay prep, manual Capture, again no chrono. (4) Once the Mimic's attempt image fully lands, the round auto-reveals to both sides simultaneously — no message needed to trigger reveal itself, since "both images present" is a fact computable identically on both sides the instant the second img-end lands. (5) Only the Poser can rate; the Mimic's UI is locked to a waiting state (same phase value on both sides, branching on isPoser — same pattern as Doodle Duel's isMyTurnToDraw). (6) Either side may click "Next round" once a verdict exists — this IS turn-gated in the sense of needing a network message (see copycat-next-round), because advancing local-only state per client is exactly the bug class already hit twice (duel-next-round, then independently avoided in Mind Match). Round-to-round, the Poser role alternates strictly by round-index parity — poserIsInitiatorForRound(index) = index % 2 === 0 — computed identically on both sides and never sent over the wire, exact mirror of drawerIsInitiatorForRound in use-duel-session.ts.
specs.singleAuthority: No synced-randomness need exists in this design at all — there is no shuffle, no deck, no dice. The only "who decides" question is role assignment, and that's solved the same way Doodle Duel solves it: poserIsInitiatorForRound(roundIndex) is a pure function of the round index, computed independently and identically by both peers from state each already has (their own isInitiator flag + the shared roundIndex, which itself only ever advances via the guarded copycat-next-round message — see pitfalls). It is never transmitted as a value, so there's nothing to desync or forge. Beyond role assignment, the Poser holds two distinct authorities per round, both for the same reason Doodle Duel gives judging authority to the drawer: only they know their own intent. (a) Content authority — only the Poser's captured still becomes "the reference" for that round; the Mimic cannot submit a reference, cannot skip the Poser's step, and cannot see anything until the Poser's image is confirmed complete. (b) Verdict authority — only the Poser submits copycat-rate; the Mimic has no rating UI at all (not just disabled — not rendered), because a self- or Mimic-issued verdict would be judging against an intent the Mimic can't see. Deliberately, nobody is the authority over a clock, because there is no clock — this is a design choice as explicit as Word Sonar's "whoever is asked answers locally," stated here so it isn't mistaken for an oversight: Copy Cat has no round timer in any phase, on purpose, mirroring the exact lesson from Duo Doodle's failed live-during-capture placement (time pressure kills a mimicry/expression game even more than it killed in-session doodling).
messageTypes: { t: "copycat-hello" } — sent once by the guest the instant their message listener is attached, before anything else. Same job as duel-hello: proves the guest's dataChannel listener exists before the host (always Poser of round 0, since poserIsInitiatorForRound(0) === true) fires the very first copycat-round-start. Without this, round 0 can start before the guest's React effect has mounted its handler — the exact class of race the photo flow's hello/config handshake was originally built to close.

{ t: "copycat-round-start"; round: number; poserIsInitiator: boolean } — sent by whichever side is about to pose, the moment they enter the posing screen (NOT gated behind any 'ready' countdown). Purely informational: lets the Mimic's UI flip from lobby/idle to 'your partner is posing now…' with a spinner. Carries no duration/deadline field at all — unlike duel-round-start, there is nothing to count down.

{ t: "copycat-img-meta"; round: number; role: "poser" | "mimic" } — begins a chunked still transfer, reusing the exact ~12KB chunking approach of lib/capture/image-transfer.ts but as CopyCat's own protocol member (never mixed with RealtimeMessage, matching the convention already established for duel/word-sonar/mindmatch protocols). round+role together let the receiver's buffer be tagged and validated against stale data (see pitfalls) instead of image-transfer.ts's untagged single ambient buffer, which is safe there only because a photo room never has two logically-distinct images in flight in the same channel lifetime the way CopyCat's poser-then-mimic sequence does.
{ t: "copycat-img-chunk"; part: string } — identical shape/semantics to the existing 'img' message; appended to the buffer opened by the most recent copycat-img-meta for that round+role.

{ t: "copycat-img-end"; round: number; role: "poser" | "mimic" } — closes the transfer. This is the ONLY message that may trigger a phase transition (posing→mimic-prep on role:"poser", mimic-prep→reveal on role:"mimic") — img-meta must never trigger a transition, see pitfalls.

{ t: "copycat-rate"; round: number; verdict: "nailed-it" | "close" | "not-quite" } — sent ONLY by the Poser after seeing both stills side by side; three-tier rather than binary so the recap has some texture (a straight pass/fail felt too thin for a photobooth-adjacent game). The Mimic-side UI has no code path that can construct or send this message.

{ t: "copycat-next-round"; round: number } — sent by whichever side clicks 'Next round' / 'See recap' first, exact mirror of duel-next-round / wordsonar-advance / mindmatch-advance. Carries the round number being left so a duplicate/late copy of the message (e.g. both sides click within the same tick) can be ignored by the receiving side if it no longer matches roundIndexRef.current, on top of a local roundAdvancedRef guard against double-firing on the sending side itself.
syncPitfalls: Phase transition must gate on img-end, never img-meta. If the Mimic's UI flipped to mimic-prep as soon as copycat-img-meta arrived (before all chunks landed), the ghost overlay would render a partial/corrupt JPEG data URL for however long the transfer takes. use-capture-session.ts already treats a received image as atomic only at its 'img-end' equivalent — this design keeps that invariant explicit rather than re-deriving it under time pressure later.

Stale-buffer collision across the poser→mimic handoff within one round, and across rounds. Two chunked transfers happen per round (poser's reference, then mimic's attempt) over the same channel — a naive single ambient buffer (as lib/capture/image-transfer.ts uses, safe there because a photo room only ever has one image class in flight) would let a late-arriving chunk from the poser's transfer corrupt the mimic's buffer if the two overlapped even briefly, or let a straggler chunk from round N corrupt round N+1's transfer after a fast advance. Fix: the receiver keys its buffer by (round, role) taken from img-meta/img-end, and discards/warns on any img chunk that doesn't match the currently-open (round, role) pair instead of silently appending it.

Round-advance needs its own idempotency-guarded network message, exactly the bug class hit twice already (duel-next-round's discovery, then deliberately avoided up front in Mind Match's mindmatch-advance). Without copycat-next-round, each side would locally increment its own roundIndex on click — a double-click, or both partners clicking their own 'Next round' within the same window, desyncs the round counter and therefore desyncs which side is poserIsInitiatorForRound. Guard: a roundAdvancedRef flip on the sender plus a round-number check on the receiver (ignore a copycat-next-round for a round already left).

Ghost-overlay mirroring mismatch — a visual-correctness trap, not a network race, but just as real. capture-frame.ts's `mirrored` option de-mirrors a self-capture so the STORED data URL is in true (non-mirrored, 'how others see you') orientation — both the Poser's reference and the Mimic's attempt are captured this way, which is correct for the final side-by-side/recap/export. But the Mimic's live <video> preview on screen is still CSS-mirrored (standard selfie-preview convention, same as everywhere else in this app). Overlaying the true-orientation reference directly on top of the mirrored live preview would put the reference's 'their right hand' on the opposite screen side from the Mimic's own mirrored right hand, making 'copy this pose' spatially backwards and confusing. Fix: apply a DISPLAY-ONLY `scaleX(-1)` to the ghost overlay element itself (never to the underlying data URL used for rating/recap/export) so it lines up with the Mimic's own mirrored self-view.

No self-rating and no rating deadlock. Only the Poser can construct copycat-rate (the Mimic's screen never renders rating controls at all, not merely disabled) — but if the Poser disconnects between reveal and rating, the Mimic must not spin forever waiting for a verdict that will never arrive. Reuse the same category of fix J5 already built for the photo flow (dataChannel-becomes-null detection driving a 'partner disconnected' banner + resend-link CTA) rather than inventing a bespoke timeout here.

Poser role must stay a pure function of roundIndex, never a transmitted flag. copycat-round-start's poserIsInitiator field is carried for the same 'explicit over implicit, we've been burned before' robustness reason duel-round-start keeps drawerIsInitiator despite being redundant with parity — but the actual source of truth both sides render from is the local poserIsInitiatorForRound(roundIndex) computation, not the received field, so a dropped/duplicated copycat-round-start can't flip who's allowed to pose.

Double-capture guard on the Poser side. A fast double-click on 'Capture' before the first send completes must not fire two independent copycat-img-meta/…/img-end sequences for the same round — guard identically to the round-advance guard (a capturedForRoundRef flip checked before starting a transfer), otherwise the Mimic's receiver could see a second img-meta arrive mid-assembly of the first and corrupt its buffer even with the (round, role) keying above.
specs.uiNotes: Phases (types/copy-cat.ts, CopyCatPhase): "lobby" (waiting room, same shell as Duel/Word Sonar/Mind Match lobbies, 'How it works' explainer per the lesson already learned on Doodle Duel's missing rules notice) → "posing" (Poser: own live camera + big manual Capture button, no countdown anywhere on screen; Mimic: 'Your partner is posing…' spinner state, camera bubble still visible via the shared FaceBubbles.tsx so nobody's video/audio drops mid-game, same fix already applied to Duel/Mind Match) → "mimic-prep" (Mimic: own live camera with the reference photo rendered as a semi-transparent — config.copyCat.ghostOpacity, ~0.35 — display-mirrored overlay per the pitfall above, plus a manual Capture button, no countdown; Poser: 'Your partner is copying you…' waiting state, deliberately NOT given a live peek of the Mimic's camera during this phase, so the reveal genuinely reveals something rather than being anticlimactic) → "reveal" (both sides: the two stills side by side, reference labeled and attempt labeled, full width on mobile stacking to top/bottom; Poser only: three verdict buttons — Nailed it / Close / Not quite — rendered, Mimic: those buttons are simply absent, replaced by 'Waiting for the verdict…') → after the last round, "recap" (score tally header — count of each verdict tier — then one card per round: reference thumbnail + attempt thumbnail + verdict badge, composed on canvas via lib/copy-cat/compose-recap.ts mirroring lib/doodle-duel/compose-recap.ts's per-round-transparent-canvas-composited-onto-white-background approach, downloadable/shareable via the existing shareOrDownload helper, plus a Replay button following DuelClient's replay() precedent — same connection, no renegotiation, round 0 resets to whichever side is poserIsInitiatorForRound(0)). Suggested file layout matching existing game conventions: types/copy-cat.ts + types/copy-cat-realtime.ts, hooks/use-copy-cat-session.ts, components/copy-cat/{CopyCatClient,CopyCatLobby,CopyCatRoundStage,CopyCatGhostOverlay,CopyCatRecap}.tsx, lib/copy-cat/compose-recap.ts, app/[locale]/copycat/{page.tsx, join/page.tsx, r/[code]/page.tsx}, plus one new entry in lib/games/registry.ts: kind "copycat", prefix "C" (unused — existing prefixes are P/D/W/M), roomPath "/copycat/r", joinPath "/copycat/join", createPath "/copycat", name "Copy Cat", a Lucide icon such as Copy or Repeat2, promoNamespace "landing.copyCat". config additions: config.copyCat.rounds (suggest 4, even — unlike Doodle Duel's odd-round tie-avoidance reasoning, Copy Cat wants an EVEN round count so the poser/mimic split is exactly 50/50 fair rather than off-by-one) and config.copyCat.ghostOpacity.
specs.rules: Copy Cat is a 2-player, no-timer photobooth mimicry game played after connecting (same room-code/WebRTC handshake as every other SnapLover room). A match is config.copyCat.rounds rounds (suggested: 4, even, for an exact 50/50 Poser/Mimic split across the match). Round index parity alone decides the Poser for that round — poserIsInitiatorForRound(index) = index % 2 === 0 — computed independently and identically on both peers, never transmitted, exact analog of Doodle Duel's drawer alternation. Each round has exactly one directional handoff, never simultaneous or back-and-forth action: (1) The Poser strikes any pose/expression on their own live camera and presses Capture whenever ready — no countdown, no time limit, by explicit design (the mirror-image of the lesson that killed the original in-session Duo Doodle placement: forcing a clock onto an expression/mimicry moment kills it). Their still is captured via the existing capture-frame.ts (with mirrored:true, storing true/non-mirrored orientation) and streamed to the Mimic via chunked transfer reusing image-transfer.ts's ~12KB-chunk approach under Copy Cat's own message types. (2) The instant the Mimic's receiver sees the transfer's closing message, their screen shows their own live camera with the reference photo composited on top as a semi-transparent 'ghost' (opacity ~35%, display-mirrored to match their own mirrored self-view — see UI notes), and they press their own Capture whenever they feel their pose matches, again with no time limit. Their still streams back to the Poser the same way. (3) The instant both stills exist on both sides, the round auto-reveals: reference and attempt shown side by side to both players. (4) Only the Poser — the one person who actually knows what they were going for — submits a verdict: Nailed it / Close / Not quite. The Mimic cannot rate their own attempt; their screen shows a waiting state until the verdict lands. (5) Either player may then advance to the next round (or, after the final round, to the recap); doing so sends a dedicated idempotency-guarded network message so the very first click — from either side — advances both screens together, rather than each side incrementing a local counter (the exact desync class already hit on Doodle Duel and pre-empted on Mind Match). The match recap shows a tally of verdicts across all rounds plus a per-round card (reference thumbnail, attempt thumbnail, verdict), downloadable/shareable as a composed PNG through the same shareOrDownload helper the other games already use, with a Replay option that restarts a fresh match on the same connection without renegotiating WebRTC.

specs.name: Reflex Match
specs.rules:
GOAL: best-of-7 rounds (config.reflex.rounds = 7), first to strictly more round-wins after 7 rounds takes the match; a 3.5–3.5-impossible tie (since 7 is odd this can't literally tie on points, but draw rounds — see below — can leave both at e.g. 3-3 with one round void) triggers sudden-death: repeat single rounds until one round has a decisive (non-draw) winner.

GRID: fixed 3x3 grid (9 cells) every round — no size ramp in v1, keep the perceptual task constant so difficulty comes from tension/reflex, not rules complexity. Each cell renders one procedural shape via a new `lib/reflex-match/paint-shape.ts` (same "pure config, no image assets" approach as `lib/frames/paint.ts`): shape enum (circle/square/triangle/diamond/star), hue, rotationDeg. All 8 non-odd cells share identical shape+hue+rotation; exactly one cell (the odd one) differs in exactly one property, chosen per round from {rotation offset ~25-40deg, hue shift ~15-20deg, added notch} so the difference is real but not trivial to spot at a glance.

ROUND FLOW:
1. Round N's authority peer (deduced by parity, never transmitted — `authorityIsInitiatorForRound(round) = round % 2 === 0`, exact same pattern as Doodle Duel's `drawerIsInitiatorForRound`) generates a fresh random 32-bit seed (`Math.random() * 2**31 | 0`) and a synced reveal instant `revealAt` = its own local clock + `config.reflex.leadMs` (1200ms "get ready" flash, shorter than the photo countdown since there's no 3-2-1 to display — just a pulsing placeholder grid).
2. Authority sends `reflex-round-start` immediately. CRITICAL: neither side computes or renders the actual shape grid on receipt — both schedule a local timer for `revealAt` converted through the existing clock-sync offset (reuse `lib/realtime/schedule-capture.ts`'s scheduling primitive verbatim, the same one driving the photo countdown), and only at that fired timeout does either side call the pure `generateRound(seed, gridSize)` function and paint. This applies to authority's own client too — it does NOT get to pre-render just because it minted the seed first.
3. At the scheduled instant, both clients render the identical grid (same seed, same deterministic function) and taps become valid.
4. Each client watches its own taps locally. A tap before local render (or timestamped earlier than `revealAt`) is a false start — ignored, tapper gets a brief "too early" shake, no message sent. A tap on a non-odd cell is a miss — brief shake, no message sent, player may keep tapping. The FIRST tap a client registers on the correct odd cell is timestamped (synced clock) and sent once as `reflex-tap`; further taps that round are ignored client-side.
5. Authority peer collects both its own local correct-tap (if any) and the peer's `reflex-tap` message (if any), waiting up to `config.reflex.roundTimeoutMs` (5000ms) from `revealAt`. Winner = whoever's synced tap timestamp is earlier; if only one side ever tapped correctly, they win by default; if neither tapped in time, the round is a draw (void — no point awarded, but it still consumes one of the 7 rounds). Authority broadcasts `reflex-round-result` once, exactly once per round.
6. Either player clicks "Next round" — first click wins, guarded by an idempotency ref so a double-click or two near-simultaneous clicks (one per screen) don't desync round counters (same fix class as Doodle Duel's `duel-next-round` bug and Mind Match's `mindmatch-advance`).
specs.turnModel: Not turn-based in the exclusive sense — every round is a simultaneous free-for-all tap race, both players acting the instant the synced reveal fires, nobody waits for the other to "go." The only alternation is which peer holds round-authority (deduced by round-index parity, exactly like Doodle Duel's drawer role), and that authority governs seed generation + result arbitration only, never who's allowed to tap or when — tapping itself is never gated on turn order, matching the lesson from Word Sonar (guessing isn't turn-gated) and avoiding the mistake of modeling a reflex race as artificial turns just because "someone has to go first" feels natural.
specs.singleAuthority: Round N's authority peer (host on even rounds, guest on odd — parity-deduced locally by both sides, identical to `drawerIsInitiatorForRound`, never sent over the wire) is the sole authority for exactly two things: (1) minting that round's random seed, and (2) arbitrating the round's winner by comparing both sides' synced tap timestamps and broadcasting the one canonical `reflex-round-result`. The non-authority peer cannot be cheated on either count: the seed is a single small integer, and the resulting grid — including which cell is odd — is a pure deterministic function (`generateRound(seed, gridSize)`) that both clients execute themselves from the same input, so authority cannot alter "which cell is correct" after the fact without also changing the seed it already sent (and a changed/resent seed for the same round number is trivially rejected as stale/invalid by the non-authority client). Authority also cannot silently give itself a head-start: rendering is gated behind the shared `revealAt` synced timestamp on BOTH clients equally (via the existing clock-sync offset primitive), so authority computing the grid locally a few ms before the message reaches the peer confers no advantage — it still isn't allowed to render or accept taps before the same wall-clock instant the peer is scheduled for. The only thing authority is trusted for that peer cannot independently verify is the arbitration comparison itself — mitigated by `reflex-round-result` including both raw timestamps (host and guest), so the losing side can see the actual numbers and the difference is auditable/visible in the UI, not a black box.
messageTypes: reflex-round-start { round: number; seed: number; revealAt: number } — sent once by that round's authority peer immediately at round start; revealAt is a synced-clock timestamp (authority's local clock + config.reflex.leadMs), converted by each receiver through the existing clock-sync offset before scheduling its local reveal timer, never used as a raw receipt-time trigger.

reflex-tap { round: number; cellIndex: number; tapAt: number } — sent by EITHER peer (both run identical logic, not just the non-authority side), exactly once per round, only on that client's first tap landing on the correct odd cell at or after its local revealAt; false starts and misses are never networked.

reflex-round-result { round: number; winner: 'host' | 'guest' | 'draw'; hostTapAt: number | null; guestTapAt: number | null; oddIndex: number } — sent exactly once per round, by authority only, after collecting both taps or hitting roundTimeoutMs; oddIndex is redundant (both sides already computed it) but included so the UI can highlight/confirm the correct cell without re-deriving it, and so a client that somehow diverged can flag a desync rather than silently disagree.

reflex-advance { round: number } — sent by whichever peer clicks 'Next round' first; guarded on both ends by an idempotency ref (advancedRef) so a double-click or a near-simultaneous click from each screen advances the shared round counter exactly once, not twice.
syncPitfalls: Render-on-receipt would give authority a free reaction-time head start every single round (it always knows the seed at least one network hop before the peer does, since it generates it locally first) — fixed by never rendering on message receipt at all; both clients, authority included, gate rendering and tap-acceptance behind the same clock-sync-adjusted revealAt instant, reusing the exact scheduling primitive already proven for the photo countdown (lib/realtime/schedule-capture.ts) rather than inventing a second one.

A tap timestamped before revealAt (a lucky guess on rhythm, or a client clock drift edge case) must be discarded as a false start rather than accepted at face value — otherwise a player could learn to 'beat' the reveal by tapping blind on a fixed rhythm without ever seeing the grid.

Same 'no confirmation before an action resolves' trap as Word Sonar's turn-gated guess and Doodle Duel's next-round bug, inverted: it would be tempting to model this as authority-announces-winner-then-waits-for-ack before advancing, but 'Next round' needs its own idempotency-guarded message (reflex-advance) for the same reason duel-next-round needed one — without it, one client could advance locally on receiving reflex-round-result while the other advances locally on its own button click, double-advancing the shared round counter if both fire near-simultaneously.

Consuming the seed's PRNG draws in a different order on each client (e.g. one side computes oddIndex before shape params, the other after) would silently desync which cell is 'odd' between host and guest despite both having the correct seed — generateRound(seed, gridSize) must be one pure, single-source-of-truth function imported by both sides, never independently reimplemented per client, with a fixed draw order documented in the function itself.

Trusting authority's own local tap timestamp without also trusting the peer's requires authority to actually wait out roundTimeoutMs before declaring a unilateral win when it received no reflex-tap message — a naive implementation might have authority declare victory the instant its own tap fires, without giving the peer's message time to arrive over the data channel, incorrectly turning ordinary network latency into a false loss for the peer.

specs.name: Bingo
specs.turnModel: No turns at all, and nothing is turn-gated. There are exactly two concurrent activities per round: (1) the caller's interval broadcast of one drawn number every callIntervalMs, driven by a timer, not by any 'your turn' exchange; (2) both players — including the caller — auto-marking their own private card the instant a number they hold gets called, and pressing a 'BINGO !' claim button the moment their own card locally shows a completed line. Marking and claiming are simultaneous and symmetric for both peers; the only asymmetry is who currently owns number-generation authority for this round (see singleAuthority), which has nothing to do with turns and never gates an action the other side wants to take. This directly avoids the turn-gating mistake made twice before (Doodle Duel's next-round desync, Word Sonar's turn-gated guess): claiming is never blocked on 'waiting your turn', because the mechanic never had turns to begin with.
specs.singleAuthority: Per round, exactly one peer is 'the caller', chosen by round parity — round % 2 === 0 → host calls, else guest calls (callerIsInitiatorForRound(round), derived identically and locally on both sides from the round index alone, never transmitted — same pattern as Doodle Duel's drawerIsInitiatorForRound). The caller is the sole authority for exactly one thing: generating and pacing the shared 1-75 draw order for that round. Concretely: the caller locally Fisher-Yates-shuffles the full 1-75 range using local crypto randomness, then immediately (before calling the first number) broadcasts a commitment — SHA-256(salt + fullSequence.join(',')) plus a fresh random salt kept secret client-side — via bingo-draw-commit. It then broadcasts one number at a time on the interval. This is a commit-then-reveal scheme, the exact pattern this brief flags as acceptable ('the generating peer commits to it in a way that can't be silently changed'): the caller is trusted to have fixed the whole order before play starts and to call strictly in that order, and the other side is given equivalent trust not by seeing the order upfront (that would leak future numbers and let players game the claim-button race) but by being able to catch any deviation after the fact — see syncPitfalls #6 for the exact verification. Card generation itself needs NO cross-peer authority: each player generates their own 5x5 card fully locally and never transmits it (nothing to keep in sync, no incentive to cheat a card only you ever see). Claim verification also has no single authority: both sides — including the caller — independently verify any bingo-claim against their own copy of the append-only called-numbers log, so the caller's role never extends to 'deciding who won'.
messageTypes: bingo-hello — {} — proves the receiving peer's listener is attached before the caller starts round 1 or resumes after a reconnect (same role as photo's hello / duel-hello, never trust dataChannel.onopen for this).

bingo-round-start — { round: number; callerIsInitiator: boolean } — sent by whichever peer becomes caller this round, right after both sides have exchanged bingo-hello; callerIsInitiator is redundant with round parity but kept explicit (this codebase has been bitten before by trusting an implicit parity deduction alone).
bingo-draw-commit — { round: number; commitHash: string } — the caller's cryptographic commitment to its full (not-yet-revealed) 75-number draw order, sent before the first number is called.

bingo-number-called — { round: number; index: number; number: number } — one broadcast per interval tick; index is the 0-based position in the draw order, letting a reconnecting or freshly-caught-up peer detect any gap.

bingo-claim — { round: number; line: { type: 'row'|'col'|'diag'; index: number }; lineNumbers: number[] } — sent by EITHER peer (caller or guesser) the instant their own card shows a completed line; lineNumbers discloses only the 5 (or 4 + free space) numbers on that specific line, never the rest of the card, so a claim is fully checkable without breaking card privacy.

bingo-draw-reveal — { round: number; salt: string; fullSequence: number[] } — sent by the caller once the round has ended (by claim or by exhausting all 75 draws), letting both sides retroactively hash-verify the commitment and confirm every broadcast number matched the pre-committed order.

bingo-next-round — { round: number } — sent by the first peer to click 'Manche suivante'/'Voir le récap'; carries the round index so a near-simultaneous second click on the other screen is recognized as a duplicate and ignored (same idempotency-guard pattern that fixed the real duel-next-round desync bug, applied here from day one instead of being rediscovered).

bingo-resync — { round: number; calledNumbers: number[]; commitHash: string } — sent by the caller when a reconnect's bingo-hello arrives mid-round; replays the ENTIRE called-numbers log so far (not a delta) so the reconnecting peer's card can catch up in one pass, then the caller resumes live interval broadcasting from where it left off.
syncPitfalls: Turn-gating the claim or the marking: neither is gated on any notion of turn — both peers mark and may claim at any instant a broadcast number makes it possible, avoiding the exact class of bug already found twice (Doodle Duel next-round, Word Sonar turn-gated guess).

Missing idempotency guard on manual round advance: bingo-next-round carries the round index and is checked against a roundAdvancedRef exactly like duel-next-round's fix, applied from the start rather than waiting to hit the same bug a third time.

Stale closures over round/calledNumbers/commitHash/card in the data-channel message handler: use-bingo-session.ts's handler is mounted once (deps [dataChannel]) and must read all round-scoped state through refs kept current by dedicated effects, exactly the fix class already documented for both use-capture-session.ts and use-duel-session.ts — applied proactively here since it is now a known recurring bug shape in this codebase.

Stale card/draw-order bleeding into the next round: resetRoundState() must regenerate a fresh local card AND (when about to be caller) a fresh shuffle+commitment at the start of every round, called both from the initial round-start path and the about-to-become-caller transition — mirrors the real Doodle Duel bug where a peer briefly saw their own previous drawing on becoming drawer again.

Resuming a dropped connection on dataChannel.onopen instead of a proven-listening handshake: reconnection triggers on receiving bingo-hello (proof the peer's new listener is actually attached), never on onopen, which guarantees nothing about the other side — the caller then replays the full calledNumbers log via bingo-resync so the reconnecting card catches up in one shot instead of missing however many numbers were called while it was down.

Caller draw-order bias (the genuinely new risk this brief calls out): because the caller already knows their own card before generating the shared draw order, an unconstrained caller could silently favor their own numbers early or stall the opponent's. Fixed with commit-then-reveal: the caller hashes salt+fullSequence and broadcasts only the hash before calling anything; every peer records the actually-broadcast prefix in order; at round end the caller reveals salt+fullSequence and both sides (independently) recompute the hash AND diff the revealed sequence's prefix against their own recorded broadcast order. A hash mismatch or a prefix mismatch proves the caller deviated from what it originally committed to (SHA-256 preimage resistance means it cannot retroactively fabricate a matching salt+sequence). Explicitly acknowledged limitation given the no-trusted-server constraint: detection is real and both sides get it, but there is no enforcement mechanism beyond surfacing a 'fairness check failed' notice — the already-decided round outcome is not retroactively reversed, same category of trust limit already accepted everywhere else in this P2P design.

Simultaneous/near-simultaneous claims from both peers: NOT resolved by 'whichever bingo-claim message physically arrived first' (a real network race, and asymmetric per peer since the two claims could be received in different order/timing on each side). Instead both sides independently recompute, from their own identical calledNumbers log, the exact index at which each claimed line's numbers all became covered (max of each number's position in the log), and take the lower index as winner — fully deterministic and identical on both sides regardless of message arrival order. An exact tie on that computed index is declared a draw for the round, credited to both.

Card privacy vs. claim verifiability tension: a claim discloses only the specific completed line's numbers, never the rest of the card — enough for the other side to fully verify (line's numbers ⊆ calledNumbers so far) without breaking the same 'never transmit the private board' default already used for secret words in Word Sonar.
specs.uiNotes: Two-phase round UI reusing the established scaffolding (FaceBubbles.tsx for the persistent camera bubbles, no prénom/config input — same generic 'Toi'/'Partenaire' scope choice already made for Doodle Duel and Mind Match). Round-start: brief synchronized 'Get ready' countdown (reusing the existing Countdown component pattern) rather than a per-side manual start button — unlike Doodle Duel's word-pick, the caller has no secret content to reveal before starting, so there is no reason to gate on an explicit click; the countdown itself keeps the lesson ('never start a timer by surprise') satisfied since both sides see it together. Calling phase: both players see an identical layout regardless of caller/guesser role — a large 'current number' tile, a horizontal history strip of all numbers called so far, their own 5x5 card below with the free center cell pre-marked and other cells auto-lighting the instant a matching number is called (auto-marking chosen over manual marking to keep this casual and quick, consistent with the app's tone), and a 'BINGO !' claim button that stays disarmed until the local card actually shows a completed line — arming it automatically but still requiring the press (preserves the genre's 'shout it' moment and creates genuine race tension when both cards complete near the same call, without ever gating who is allowed to press). Round-end: reveals the winning line highlighted on the winner's card, runs the silent fairness check (surfacing a small non-blocking badge only on failure), and shows 'Manche suivante' with the idempotency-guarded network message. After config.bingo.rounds (3, matching Doodle Duel's round count) rounds, a recap screen (lib/bingo/compose-recap.ts, components/bingo/BingoRecap.tsx) — one row per round (winner + winning line type) plus a running score header including any draws, footer brand mark, downloadable/shareable via the existing lib/share-or-download.ts helper, exactly the recap pattern already shared by Doodle Duel and Mind Match. Registry entry: kind 'bingo', prefix 'B' (free, no collision with existing P/D/W), roomPath '/bingo/r', joinPath '/bingo/join', createPath '/bingo', icon Grid3x3 (visually reads as a card grid at a glance in the games-hub list, distinct from Palette/Radar), promoNamespace 'landing.bingo' — landing promotion itself deferred pending the same unified-'Games' section decision already open for Doodle Duel/Mind Match, not a new one-off section.
specs.rules:
OVERVIEW
Bingo is the third mini-game in the hub, after Doodle Duel (asymmetric drawer/guesser) and Word Sonar (symmetric-turn letter battleship). It is symmetric in gameplay (both players do the same thing at the same time — generate a card, mark it, try to claim a line) but asymmetric in authority for exactly one piece of shared state per round: who generates and paces the drawn-number stream. Routes: /bingo (create), /bingo/join, /bingo/r/[code], root component BingoClient.tsx — same shape as Doodle Duel/Mind Match. No prénom/config capture on create (matches the established 'no scope creep' choice for both prior games): a single 'Créer un Bingo' button, generic 'Toi'/'Partenaire' labels throughout.

CARD GENERATION (per player, per round, fully local — never transmitted)
Standard 5x5 bingo card, columns B-I-N-G-O with fixed number ranges: B=1-15, I=16-30, N=31-45, G=46-60, O=61-75. Each column draws 5 unique random numbers from its range (4 for the N column), center cell (row 2, col 2, index 12 of 25) is the free space, pre-marked from the start and always counted as satisfied in any line that includes it. Generated with local crypto randomness (crypto.getRandomValues via a Fisher-Yates over each column's 15-value range, take first 5/4). No fairness concern here: a card is private to its owner, shown to nobody else, so there is zero incentive or opportunity to cheat your own card — the only genuinely shared, contested resource is the draw order (see below).

CALLER SELECTION
callerIsInitiatorForRound(round) = round % 2 === 0 (host calls on even rounds, guest on odd) — pure function of the round index, computed identically and independently on both sides, never sent over the wire, exactly mirroring Doodle Duel's drawerIsInitiatorForRound.

DRAW ORDER GENERATION + FAIRNESS (the core new design problem this game raises)
At the start of a round, the caller (and ONLY the caller) generates a full random permutation of 1-75 locally (Fisher-Yates, crypto randomness). Because the caller already knows their own card's numbers, an unconstrained caller could silently bias this order (call their own numbers early, delay the opponent's) with zero way for the guesser to detect it in real time. This is solved with a commit-then-reveal scheme rather than any 2-party shared-seed protocol (which would contradict the 'sole caller' framing and add needless complexity):
  1. Before calling any number, the caller computes commitHash = SHA-256(salt + fullSequence.join(',')) with a fresh random salt kept client-side, and broadcasts { round, commitHash } via bingo-draw-commit.
  2. The caller then broadcasts one number at a time via bingo-number-called ({ round, index, number }) every config.bingo.callIntervalMs (suggested 3500ms). Both players — including the caller itself, for its own card — append every received number, in order, to a local calledNumbers[] log and mark their card against it live.
  3. The round ends either when a bingo-claim is accepted (see below) or, as a formality safety net, once all 75 numbers have been called (statistically near-impossible to reach without an earlier line completion, given a 5-in-a-line requirement over a 25-cell card).
  4. Immediately once the round ends, the caller broadcasts bingo-draw-reveal ({ round, salt, fullSequence }). Both sides (again, including the caller, for self-consistency) recompute SHA-256(salt + fullSequence.join(',')) and check it equals the earlier commitHash, AND check that fullSequence.slice(0, calledNumbers.length) deep-equals their own live-recorded calledNumbers array in exact order. A hash mismatch or an order mismatch means the caller deviated from what it originally committed to before play started — SHA-256's preimage resistance means it cannot retroactively fabricate a matching salt+sequence after the fact, so any deviation is provably caught, not just suspected. On failure, show a small non-blocking 'fairness check failed' notice (console.warn with details); the round's already-decided outcome is NOT reversed retroactively — this game has no trusted server to enforce anything beyond detection, an explicitly accepted limitation consistent with the rest of this P2P architecture.
Why this gives the guesser equivalent trust without seeing the order upfront: revealing the full order before the round ends would let a player pre-know which future numbers complete which line, letting them time their 'BINGO !' press artificially instead of reacting to their card lighting up in real time — a real competitive advantage given claiming is manual. Commit-then-reveal gives verifiability without that leak.

CLAIMING A LINE
Any of the 5 rows, 5 columns, or 2 diagonals counts as a winning line (free space always counts as satisfied). The instant a player's own card shows a completed line, their client arms (but does not auto-press) a 'BINGO !' button; pressing it broadcasts bingo-claim ({ round, line: { type, index }, lineNumbers }) where lineNumbers is only the 4-5 real numbers on that specific line (free space excluded from the payload, it needs no verification) — this discloses the minimum necessary to prove the claim, not the rest of the card, preserving the same 'card never leaves the device except what's needed to verify' principle Word Sonar uses for secret words.
Verification, run independently and identically by BOTH peers (caller and guesser alike) — no single arbiter: on receiving (or on producing) a claim, check every number in lineNumbers appears in the local calledNumbers log; if any number is missing, the claim is invalid and silently ignored (no round-trip 'rejected' message needed — an invalid claim simply never becomes a winner on the receiving side, so a lying peer gains nothing). For a valid claim, compute completingIndex = max(calledNumbers.indexOf(n) for n in lineNumbers) — the position in the shared draw order at which this specific line became fully covered. If both peers produce a valid claim in the same round (near-simultaneous line completions), each side independently compares its own completingIndex against the other's stated line's completingIndex (recomputed locally the same way, never trusted from the sender) and declares the lower index the winner; an exact tie is declared a draw, credited to both. This resolves the race deterministically from the shared, already-agreed-upon calledNumbers log rather than from message arrival order, which would differ per peer and could produce two different 'winners' on the two screens.

RECONNECTION
If a peer's dataChannel drops mid-round, the caller (on detecting a null data channel) pauses its calling interval — broadcasting into the void while nobody can mark is pointless and unfair. On reconnect, the returning peer sends bingo-hello (never trusting dataChannel.onopen, which proves nothing about the other side's listener actually being attached — same lesson already documented for photo/duel reconnects); the caller responds with bingo-resync ({ round, calledNumbers, commitHash }), replaying the FULL log so far (not a delta) so the returning card can catch up in one pass, then resumes live interval broadcasting. Known, explicitly accepted limitation: if the CALLER's own tab/process is what drops (not the guesser), the committed draw order, salt, and calledNumbers log exist only in that peer's React memory (no database, per this app's architecture) and are lost on a full reload — recoverable only by restarting the round fresh with a newly generated card/order, same category of limitation already accepted elsewhere in this in-memory-only design (no attempt made here to solve authority-holder-reload recovery, since no other game in this codebase solves the equivalent case either).

ROUNDS, SCORING, RECAP
config.bingo.rounds = 3 (matches Doodle Duel), caller alternates every round by parity. Score tracked as roundsWon per player plus roundsDrawn; 'Manche suivante' advance uses bingo-next-round ({ round }) with a roundAdvancedRef idempotency guard (applying the duel-next-round fix pattern from day one rather than waiting to hit the same desync bug a third time in this codebase). After the final round, a recap screen (lib/bingo/compose-recap.ts + components/bingo/BingoRecap.tsx, canvas-composed like the other recaps) lists one row per round (winner or draw, winning line type), a score header, and the brand footer — downloadable/shareable via the existing shared lib/share-or-download.ts helper.

CONSTANTS (web/src/lib/config.ts, config.bingo)
rounds: 3, callIntervalMs: 3500, cardSize: 5, columns: [{letter:'B',min:1,max:15}, {letter:'I',min:16,max:30}, {letter:'N',min:31,max:45}, {letter:'G',min:46,max:60}, {letter:'O',min:61,max:75}], freeSpaceIndex: 12, maxDraws: 75.

FILES
types/bingo-realtime.ts (BingoMessage union, isolated from RealtimeMessage/DuelMessage/WordSonarMessage exactly like the other games' protocols), hooks/use-bingo-session.ts (state machine + the ref-backed message handler), lib/bingo/card.ts (generateCard), lib/bingo/draw-order.ts (shuffle75 + completingIndex helper), lib/bingo/commit.ts (SHA-256 commit/verify via SubtleCrypto), lib/bingo/compose-recap.ts, components/bingo/{BingoClient,BingoCard,BingoCaller,BingoRecap,BingoLobby}.tsx, app/bingo/{page.tsx,join/page.tsx,r/[code]/page.tsx}. Registry: add to web/src/lib/games/registry.ts GAMES array — kind 'bingo', prefix 'B', roomPath '/bingo/r', joinPath '/bingo/join', createPath '/bingo', name 'Bingo', icon Grid3x3, promoNamespace 'landing.bingo'. i18n: new 'bingo' namespace plus 'landing.bingo' in both web/src/i18n/messages/{fr,en}.ts, same key shape as the existing games' namespaces.
